sentence: Hola, Maru.
note: This short greeting is a complete social expression; Maru names the person being greeted.

sentence: Buenos días, don Toño; hace sol esta mañana.
grammar: Hace sol is a fixed weather expression meaning 'it is sunny.'
note: Esta mañana = this morning. Don is a respectful title before a man's given name.

sentence: Buenas tardes, señora; hace calor esta tarde.
grammar: Hace calor is a fixed weather expression meaning 'it is hot.'
note: Señora = ma'am; esta tarde = this afternoon.

sentence: Buenas noches, Julia; ya estoy aquí para la cena.
grammar: Ya estoy aquí para la cena = I'm here now for dinner; an arrival frame.
note: This greets Julia on arrival in the evening. Buenas noches can also be used when leaving at night.

sentence: Hasta mañana, Ana; la clase de mañana es aquí.
grammar: La clase de mañana es aquí = tomorrow's class is here.
note: Use this farewell when you expect to meet again the next day.

sentence: Nos vemos, Paco; hasta el lunes.
part_of_speech: pronominal verb phrase used as a farewell
grammar: Learn nos vemos as a complete casual farewell.
note: Hasta el lunes = see you Monday.

sentence: —Soy Elena. —Mucho gusto, Elena; soy David.
grammar: Soy followed by a name identifies the speaker: soy David = I am David.
note: Use the whole expression when meeting someone for the first time.

sentence: —Mucho gusto, Sofía. —Igualmente, don Pedro.
note: Here igualmente returns the other person's polite introduction.

sentence: Gracias por la ayuda con mi bolsa, Leo.
grammar: Gracias por introduces the reason for thanking someone.
note: La ayuda con mi bolsa = the help with my bag.

sentence: —Gracias por el agua, Rosa. —De nada, Iván.
note: El agua = the water. De nada is a conventional response to thanks.

sentence: Un vaso de agua, por favor.
grammar: A named item followed by por favor makes a simple courteous request.
note: Un vaso de agua = a glass of water.

sentence: Perdón por la interrupción, Julia.
grammar: Por la interrupción = for the interruption.
note: Use perdón for a small interruption or mishap. Give the r in perdón one quick tongue tap.

sentence: Disculpe, señor; ¿aquí es la salida?
part_of_speech: verb used as a polite attention-getting formula
grammar: Disculpe is an usted command form, learned here as a fixed attention-getting expression.
note: Señor = sir. ¿Aquí es la salida? = Is this the exit?

sentence: —¿Es aquí, Leo? —Sí, aquí.
note: ¿Es aquí? = Is it here? The accent distinguishes affirmative sí from si, meaning 'if.'

sentence: —¿Es aquí, Rosa? —No, allá.
note: Allá = over there. No rejects the location suggested in the question.

sentence: La palabra «mesa», otra vez, por favor, maestra.
grammar: Use the named word plus otra vez, por favor as a short request for repetition.
note: La palabra = the word; mesa = table; maestra = female teacher.

sentence: La frase, más despacio, por favor, maestra.
grammar: Use this short request to ask for slower speech.
note: La frase = the phrase or sentence.

sentence: Maestra, ¿cómo se dice «window» en español?
part_of_speech: verb phrase in a fixed clarification question
grammar: Learn ¿Cómo se dice ... en español? as one question frame: 'How do you say ... in Spanish?'
note: The quoted English word is the word the learner wants in Spanish. This question does not require a general rule for se.

sentence: Maestra, ¿qué significa «ventana»?
grammar: ¿Qué significa ...? asks 'What does ... mean?'
note: Ventana = window.

sentence: Maestra, no entiendo la palabra «ventana».
grammar: Entiendo is the first-person singular present of entender. No before it makes the statement negative.
note: Connect the final vowel of no smoothly to the opening vowel of entiendo.

sentence: Hola, me llamo Lidia.
grammar: Use me llamo plus your name as a self-introduction chunk.
note: In ordinary central Mexican speech, ll in llamo uses the same consonant as y in yo ('I'); its precise realization varies.

sentence: ¿Cuál es tu nombre, por favor?
grammar: ¿Cuál es tu ...? = What is your ...? Tu addresses one person familiarly.
note: Here nombre asks for the person's given name, rather than their surname.

sentence: Mi nombre es Ana y mi apellido es Robles.
grammar: Mi ... es ... = My ... is ...; y = and.
note: Ana is the given name; Robles is the surname in this exchange.

sentence: La clase es en español, Ana.
grammar: En plus a language names the language used: en español = in Spanish.
note: Group es-pa-ñol, with stress on ñol. Ñ represents one palatal nasal consonant.

sentence: Soy de México, Elena.
grammar: Soy de ... = I am from ...
note: Group Mé-xi-co; stress Mé. In México, x has the sound of Spanish j, made at the back of the mouth.

sentence: La casa de Ana está aquí.
grammar: La ... de Ana está aquí = Ana's ... is here.
note: Group ca-sa; stress ca. Keep both a vowels clear and steady. C before a has the k sound, with little puff of air.

sentence: La leche está aquí, Ana.
grammar: Leche is feminine: la leche.
note: Group le-che; stress le. Keep both e vowels steady, without an English-style vowel glide.

sentence: El libro de Ana está aquí.
grammar: Libro is masculine: el libro.
note: Group li-bro; stress li. Keep the i vowel steady throughout.

sentence: —¿Mucho pan, Ana? —No, poco pan, por favor.
grammar: Mucho pan = a lot of bread; poco pan = a small amount of bread.
note: Group po-co; stress po. Keep both o vowels steady. Use little puff of air on p.

sentence: —¿Un libro o dos, Ana? —Uno, por favor.
part_of_speech: cardinal numeral used as a pronoun
grammar: Uno stands alone here and refers to one book. O = or; dos = two.
note: Group u-no; stress u. Keep u steady with rounded lips.

sentence: Aquí está la mesa, Ana.
grammar: Mesa is feminine: la mesa. Aquí está ... = Here is ...
note: Group me-sa; stress me. Keep the unstressed final a clear; do not reduce it to a neutral vowel.

sentence: Un tomate verde para la salsa, por favor.
grammar: Un tomate verde = one tomatillo; para la salsa = for the salsa.
note: In central Mexico, tomate verde commonly names the tomatillo. Group to-ma-te; stress ma. Keep the unstressed o and e clear. Put the tongue at the upper teeth for t, with little puff of air.

sentence: Mi teléfono está en la mesa.
grammar: Mi ... está en la mesa = My ... is on the table.
note: Group te-lé-fo-no. Stress lé, the third syllable from the end; the written accent marks it.

sentence: Un café para Ana, por favor.
grammar: Un café requests one serving of coffee. Para Ana = for Ana.
note: Group ca-fé. Stress the final syllable fé, as marked by the written accent.

sentence: La música está en mi teléfono.
grammar: Música is feminine: la música.
note: Group mú-si-ca. Stress mú, the third syllable from the end.

sentence: Hoy es sábado, Ana.
grammar: Hoy es ... = Today is ...
note: Group sá-ba-do. Stress sá, the third syllable from the end. Spanish weekday names normally use lowercase letters.

sentence: El médico está aquí, Ana.
grammar: El médico refers here to a male doctor.
note: Group mé-di-co. Stress mé, the third syllable from the end. Make d lightly with the tongue at the upper teeth.

sentence: Mi mamá está aquí, Ana.
grammar: Mi mamá = my mom.
note: Group ma-má. Stress the final syllable má; the written accent marks that stress.

sentence: Mi papá es de México.
grammar: Mi papá = my dad; es de México = is from Mexico.
note: Group pa-pá. Stress the final syllable pá. Papá means dad; mamá means mom.

sentence: Mi número de teléfono está aquí, Ana.
grammar: Número de teléfono = phone number.
note: Group nú-me-ro. Stress nú, the third syllable from the end.

sentence: El café está aquí, pero la leche está en casa.
grammar: Pero introduces a contrast between the two statements.
note: Group pe-ro; the single r between vowels is a brief tongue tap. Make a light phrase break before pero, emphasize aquí and casa as the contrasted locations, and end the second statement with a falling tone.

sentence: El perro de Ana está en casa.
grammar: El perro de Ana = Ana's dog.
note: Group pe-rro; stress pe. Written rr between vowels represents a trill, contrasting with the brief tap in pero, meaning but.

sentence: El teléfono es caro, Ana.
grammar: Es caro = is expensive.
note: Group ca-ro; stress ca. Use one brief tongue tap for the single r between vowels.

sentence: El carro de Ana está aquí.
grammar: El carro de Ana = Ana's car.
note: Group ca-rro; stress ca. Trill rr. Carro means car; caro, with a brief tap, means expensive.

sentence: Mi mamá está en casa ahora.
grammar: Ahora tells when the statement is true.
note: Group a-ho-ra; stress ho. H is silent. The single r between vowels is a brief tongue tap.

sentence: Ana, el correo de Luis está en mi teléfono.
grammar: El correo de Luis refers here to an email message from Luis.
note: Group co-rre-o; stress rre. The adjacent e and o belong to separate syllables. Trill the medial rr.

sentence: El libro rojo está en la mesa.
grammar: Rojo describes the masculine singular noun libro.
note: Group ro-jo; stress ro. Word-initial r uses a trill, although it is written with one r.

sentence: El jabón está en la mesa, Ana.
grammar: Jabón is masculine: el jabón.
note: Group ja-bón; stress bón, as the written accent indicates. Spanish j is a friction sound made at the back of the mouth, without the initial stop of English j.

sentence: Mi teléfono es para el trabajo.
grammar: Para el trabajo = for work.
note: Group tra-ba-jo; stress ba. Use the Spanish j friction sound at the back of the mouth, without the initial stop of English j.

sentence: El niño está en casa, Ana.
grammar: Niño is masculine: el niño. Niña means girl.
note: Group ni-ño; stress ni. Ñ represents one palatal nasal consonant, made with the tongue body against the hard palate.

sentence: La clase es mañana, Ana.
grammar: La clase es mañana = The class is tomorrow.
note: Group ma-ña-na; stress ña. Ñ is one palatal nasal consonant. Here mañana means tomorrow.

sentence: Ana, ¿dónde está el baño?
grammar: ¿Dónde está el ...? = Where is the ...? Use this as a location-question chunk.
note: Group ba-ño; stress ba. Ñ is one palatal nasal consonant. Baño means restroom here.

sentence: La calle de Ana está aquí.
grammar: Calle is feminine: la calle.
note: Group ca-lle; stress ca. In ordinary central Mexican speech, ll here uses the same consonant as y in yo; its precise realization varies.

sentence: La llave está en la mesa.
grammar: Llave is feminine: la llave.
note: Group lla-ve; stress lla. Initial ll here uses the same consonant as y in yo in ordinary central Mexican speech; its precise realization varies.

sentence: Ana, yo soy de México.
grammar: Yo explicitly identifies the speaker as the subject.
note: Yo is one syllable. Its initial y uses the same consonant as ll in calle and llave in ordinary central Mexican speech; its precise realization varies.

sentence: —¿Hoy, Ana? —No, ayer.
grammar: This short clarification corrects the day: hoy = today; ayer = yesterday.
note: Group a-yer; stress yer. Y begins the second syllable and uses the same consonant as ll in calle in ordinary central Mexican speech.

sentence: La tienda está aquí, Ana.
grammar: Tienda is feminine: la tienda.
note: Group tien-da; stress tien. Make initial t with the tongue against the upper teeth rather than the English position farther back. Use little puff of air.

sentence: —¿Un café, Ana? —Dos, por favor.
part_of_speech: cardinal numeral used as a pronoun
grammar: Dos refers to two coffees in this reply.
note: Dos is one syllable. After the pause before this reply, initial d has a brief closure at the upper teeth. Between vowels, Spanish d is usually softer.

sentence: El dedo de Ana está rojo.
grammar: El dedo de Ana = Ana's finger; está rojo = is red.
note: Group de-do; stress de. After el, the first d has a closure at the upper teeth. The second d, between vowels, is lighter, without a full closure.

sentence: Un poco de pan para Ana, por favor.
grammar: Un poco de pan = a little bread.
note: Pan is one syllable. Release initial p with little puff of air, avoiding the strong aspiration common in stressed English p.

sentence: Un taco para mi papá, por favor.
grammar: Un taco requests one taco.
note: Group ta-co; stress ta. Release initial t with little puff of air. Keep the tongue at the upper teeth.

sentence: El teléfono está en casa, Ana.
grammar: En casa = at home.
note: Group ca-sa; stress ca. C before a represents the k sound. Release it with little puff of air, avoiding strong English-style aspiration.

sentence: Un poco de queso para Ana, por favor.
grammar: Un poco de queso = a little cheese.
note: Group que-so; stress que. Qu before e represents the k sound; u is silent. Release k with little puff of air.

sentence: Luis es un amigo de mi papá.
grammar: Un amigo de mi papá = a friend of my dad's.
note: Link the final n of un smoothly into the initial a of amigo, without a pause. Group amigo as a-mi-go; stress mi.

sentence: Ana, el agua está en la mesa.
grammar: Agua is feminine. Immediately before this singular noun's stressed initial a, use el.
note: Link the final l of el into the initial a of agua without a pause. Group agua as a-gua; stress a.

sentence: El café es para los amigos de Ana.
grammar: Los amigos de Ana = Ana's friends; the group may be all male or mixed.
note: Link the final s of los smoothly into the initial a of amigos. Keep the s audible. Group amigos as a-mi-gos; stress mi.

sentence: El café está en la mesa, ¿verdad, Ana?
grammar: ¿Verdad? asks the listener to confirm the preceding statement.
note: Group ver-dad; stress dad. Give the short confirmation question a gentle rising ending when checking information.

sentence: ¿Qué tal, Ana?
grammar: ¿Qué tal? is a compact casual greeting.
note: Say the greeting as one short question group, with a light rising ending for an open check-in. The fixed formula stays together; Ana names the person greeted.

sentence: Ana, ¿tú eres de México?
grammar: Tú addresses one person familiarly. Tú eres de ... = You are from ...
register: Familiar tú address to a peer.
note: Tú is one stressed syllable. Its written accent distinguishes the pronoun tú, meaning you, from possessive tu, meaning your.

sentence: Mi papá es de México; él está aquí.
grammar: Él refers back to mi papá.
note: Él is one stressed syllable. The written accent distinguishes the personal pronoun él, meaning he, from the article el, meaning the.

sentence: Aquí está el libro de Ana.
grammar: Use el with a specific masculine singular noun: el libro.

sentence: Aquí está la mesa de Ana.
grammar: Use la with a specific feminine singular noun: la mesa.

sentence: Aquí están los libros de Ana.
grammar: Use los with a specific masculine plural noun. Libros = books; aquí están = here are.

sentence: Ana, las llaves están en casa.
grammar: Use las with a specific feminine plural noun. Llaves = keys; están en casa = are at home.

sentence: Hay un libro en la mesa, Ana.
grammar: Un introduces a masculine singular object that has not yet been identified. Hay un libro = There is a book.

sentence: En la casa de Ana hay una mesa.
grammar: Una introduces an unspecified feminine singular object. Hay una mesa = There is a table.

sentence: Hay unos libros en casa de Ana.
grammar: Unos introduces an unspecified group of masculine nouns: unos libros = some books. Hay also works with plural nouns.

sentence: Aquí hay unas llaves para Ana.
grammar: Unas introduces an unspecified group of feminine nouns: unas llaves = some keys.

sentence: Aquí está el problema: el teléfono no está en casa.
grammar: Problema is masculine despite ending in a: el problema.
note: No está en casa = is not at home.

sentence: El jabón está en la mano de Ana.
grammar: Mano is feminine despite ending in o: la mano.

sentence: Mi papá es un hombre de México.
grammar: Hombre is masculine although it does not end in o: un hombre.

sentence: Ana es una mujer de México.
grammar: Mujer is feminine although it does not end in a: una mujer.

sentence: Aquí está el estudiante, mi papá.
grammar: Estudiante keeps the same form for men and women. El marks this student as male.

sentence: Aquí está la estudiante, mi mamá.
grammar: La marks this student as female; estudiante has the same ending as in el estudiante.

sentence: El sábado es el día de la clase de español.
grammar: Día is masculine despite its final a: el día.
note: La clase de español = the Spanish class.

sentence: Aquí está la foto de mi mamá.
grammar: Foto is feminine despite its final o: la foto.
note: Foto is a shortened form of fotografía.

sentence: Ana, aquí está el mapa de México.
grammar: Mapa is masculine despite its final a: el mapa.

sentence: El libro es para la clase de español.
grammar: Clase is feminine although it ends in e: la clase.

sentence: El hombre y la mujer de la foto son mis hermanos.
grammar: Hermanos can mean brothers and sisters together. Son mis = are my.
note: Y = and.

sentence: Las dos mujeres de la foto son mis hermanas.
grammar: Hermanas refers to female siblings. Mujeres is the plural of mujer.

sentence: Aquí están mis padres: mi mamá y mi papá.
grammar: Padres can mean mother and father together.

sentence: La niña y el niño de la foto son mis hijos.
grammar: Hijos can refer to daughters and sons together.
note: Niña = girl; niño = boy.

sentence: La mamá y el papá de mi papá son mis abuelos.
grammar: Abuelos can refer to a grandmother and grandfather together.

sentence: Mi familia está en casa: mi mamá, mi papá y mis hermanos.
grammar: Familia is feminine singular. Use singular está even when the family includes several people.

sentence: En casa hay dos sillas.
grammar: Add s to silla to name more than one chair: sillas.

sentence: Aquí están los vasos para el agua.
grammar: Add s to vaso to form the plural vasos.

sentence: Los platos están en la mesa.
grammar: Platos is the plural of plato, a plate.

sentence: Aquí están los lápices para la clase de español.
grammar: Lápiz becomes lápices: change z to c and add es. The written accent remains.

sentence: En el baño hay dos luces.
grammar: Luz becomes luces: change z to c and add es.

sentence: Aquí están los papeles para el médico.
grammar: Add es to papel to form papeles.
note: Here papeles means documents for the medical visit.

sentence: En la tienda hay unos relojes de pulsera para mi papá.
grammar: Add es to reloj to form relojes.
note: Reloj de pulsera means wristwatch.

sentence: Unos zapatos para mi papá, por favor.
grammar: Zapatos is masculine plural: unos zapatos.

sentence: Los pantalones de Luis están en la silla.
grammar: Pantalones is masculine plural and can name one pair of pants.

sentence: Una camisa para mi papá, por favor.
grammar: Camisa is feminine: una camisa, even when the shirt is for a man.

sentence: La falda es para Ana.
grammar: Falda is feminine: la falda.

sentence: El vestido es para mi mamá.
grammar: Vestido is masculine: el vestido, even when the dress is for a woman.

sentence: La blusa de Ana es roja.
grammar: Blusa is feminine: la blusa. Roja means red and describes a feminine singular noun.

sentence: La chamarra de Luis está en casa.
grammar: Chamarra is feminine: la chamarra.
note: Chamarra is a common everyday word for a jacket in Mexico.

sentence: La camisa es verde.
grammar: Verde has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

sentence: Los vasos de Ana son verdes.
grammar: Add s to verde for plural nouns: vasos verdes. The plural form works with either gender.

sentence: La mesa de mi mamá es grande.
grammar: Grande describes size and has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

sentence: La silla de mi mamá es pequeña.
grammar: Pequeña ends in a to agree with feminine singular silla.

sentence: Mis hermanos son pequeños: Luis es un bebé y Paco es un niño.
grammar: Pequeños agrees with masculine plural hermanos. Here it describes their young age.
note: Un bebé = a baby.

sentence: Las camisas para el trabajo son nuevas.
grammar: Nuevas ends in as to agree with feminine plural camisas.

sentence: El vaso para el agua está limpio.
grammar: Limpio ends in o to agree with masculine singular vaso. Está limpio describes its current condition.

sentence: La habitación de mi mamá está limpia.
grammar: Limpia ends in a to agree with feminine singular habitación.
note: Habitación = room.

sentence: Los zapatos de Luis están sucios.
grammar: Sucios ends in os to agree with masculine plural zapatos.

sentence: La falda para el trabajo es cómoda.
grammar: Cómoda ends in a to agree with feminine singular falda.

sentence: Unos zapatos baratos para mi papá, por favor.
grammar: Baratos ends in os to agree with masculine plural zapatos.

sentence: La foto de mi familia es bonita.
grammar: Bonita agrees with feminine singular foto, despite the noun's final o.

sentence: Luis es mi hermano mayor.
grammar: Mayor describes age here, rather than physical size.

sentence: En la foto, Ana es mi hermana menor.
grammar: Menor describes age here, rather than physical size.

sentence: En casa hay comida casera.
grammar: Casera agrees with feminine singular comida.

sentence: El agua fría es para Ana.
grammar: Agua is feminine. It takes el directly before its stressed initial a in the singular, but its adjective remains feminine: fría.

sentence: Hay pan dulce para el café.
grammar: Pan is masculine; dulce has the same singular form for either gender.
note: In Mexico, pan dulce names a category of sweet baked breads.

sentence: Un vaso de leche caliente, por favor.
grammar: Leche is feminine. Caliente has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
note: Un vaso de = a glass of.

sentence: El arroz blanco está en la mesa.
grammar: Arroz is masculine and uncountable here; blanco agrees in the masculine singular.

sentence: La sopa caliente es para mi mamá.
grammar: Sopa is feminine; caliente keeps its e ending.

sentence: En la mesa hay fruta fresca.
grammar: Fruta names fruit collectively here; fresca agrees in the feminine singular.

sentence: Dos huevos para el desayuno, por favor.
grammar: Huevos is masculine plural; dos specifies two eggs.
note: Desayuno = breakfast.

sentence: Los frijoles están en un plato.
grammar: Frijoles is masculine plural: los frijoles.

sentence: Una manzana para el niño, por favor.
grammar: Manzana is feminine: una manzana.

sentence: La naranja está en el plato.
grammar: Naranja is a feminine fruit noun here: la naranja.

sentence: Las tortillas están en un plato.
grammar: Tortillas is the regular plural of feminine tortilla: las tortillas.

sentence: Tengo una pregunta, Ana.
grammar: Una introduces one unspecified question; pregunta is feminine.
note: Tengo = I have.

sentence: Un poco de arroz para el niño, por favor.
grammar: Un poco de comes before an uncountable noun to request a small amount.

sentence: En casa hay muchos vasos.
grammar: Muchos agrees with masculine plural vasos.

sentence: En la foto hay muchas mujeres de mi familia.
grammar: Muchas agrees with feminine plural mujeres.

sentence: Hay poca leche en el vaso.
grammar: Poca agrees with feminine singular leche and describes a small amount.

sentence: Un plato para Ana y otro plato para Luis, por favor.
grammar: Otro agrees with masculine singular plato and directly precedes it, without un.

sentence: La camisa es pequeña; otra talla, por favor.
grammar: Otra agrees with feminine singular talla.
note: Talla = clothing size.

sentence: El libro de Ana es el mismo de la foto.
grammar: Mismo agrees with the understood masculine singular noun libro after el.

sentence: Mi hermana y yo estamos en la misma clase.
grammar: Misma agrees with feminine singular clase.
note: Estamos en = we are in.

sentence: El vaso y el plato están limpios; ambos son para Ana.
grammar: Ambos refers back to two masculine singular objects together.

sentence: En la mesa hay un plato para cada niño.
grammar: Cada is followed by a singular noun and does not change for gender.

sentence: Yo soy médico.
grammar: Use soy with yo. A profession normally follows ser without un or una.

sentence: Ana, tú eres estudiante.
grammar: Use eres with tú. Estudiante can describe a woman without changing its ending.

sentence: Luis es mi hermano.
grammar: Use es with a singular person named as the subject.

sentence: Ana y yo somos un equipo.
grammar: Use somos when the subject includes the speaker and another person.
note: Equipo = team.

sentence: Ana y Luis son médicos.
grammar: Use son with two people named as the subject. No indefinite article is needed before their profession.

sentence: Yo soy de Puebla.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present verb and preposition
grammar: Ser de introduces a person's place of origin.
note: Puebla is a city in Mexico.

sentence: La mesa es de madera.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present verb and preposition
grammar: Ser de followed by a material identifies what an object is made of.
note: Madera = wood.

sentence: Los zapatos son de Ana.
part_of_speech: third-person plural present verb and preposition
grammar: Ser de followed by a person can identify ownership. Son agrees with plural zapatos.

sentence: Ana es mexicana.
grammar: Use ser to identify nationality.
note: Mexicana = Mexican, describing a woman.

sentence: Hoy es sábado.
grammar: Use es to identify the current day of the week.
note: Hoy = today.

sentence: El lápiz es una herramienta.
grammar: Ser identifies the category an object belongs to.
note: Herramienta = tool.

sentence: La casa de Ana es grande.
grammar: Ser presents size as a characteristic of the house.

sentence: Ana es la médica de mi mamá.
grammar: Ser identifies a person's specific role; la médica identifies the particular doctor.
note: Médica = female doctor.

sentence: La clase es en casa de Ana.
grammar: Use ser to state where an event takes place.
note: A class is an event, so its location uses ser. Estar locates people and objects.

sentence: Hola, Ana, soy Luis.
grammar: Soy followed by a name identifies the speaker.

sentence: Yo estoy bien, gracias.
grammar: Use estar for how someone feels physically at the moment.
note: Bien = well.

sentence: Ana, ¿tú estás en casa?
grammar: Use estás with tú to ask where the addressed person is.

sentence: La llave de Ana está en casa.
grammar: Use está to locate one identified object.

sentence: Ana y yo estamos en el café.
grammar: Use estamos when the located group includes the speaker.
note: El café here means the café as a meeting place.

sentence: Los niños están tranquilos ahora.
grammar: Use están for the current state of more than one person.
note: Tranquilos = calm.

sentence: La tienda está cerrada hoy.
grammar: Estar describes whether the shop is currently open or closed.
note: Cerrada = closed.

sentence: La sopa está caliente.
grammar: Use estar to describe the food's temperature at the moment.

sentence: Yo estoy listo para la clase de español.
grammar: Estar listo means to be ready for something.
note: Listo = ready, describing a male speaker; listo para = ready for.

sentence: Luis, ¿tú estás cansado?
grammar: Use estar for someone's current tiredness.
note: Cansado = tired, describing a male person.

sentence: Ana está de vacaciones.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative verb and preposition
grammar: Estar de vacaciones is a fixed expression for being on vacation.
note: Vacaciones = vacation.

sentence: En la calle hay una farmacia.
grammar: Hay introduces the existence of an unspecified person, place, or thing.
note: Farmacia = pharmacy.

sentence: En la mesa hay dos vasos.
grammar: Hay stays the same before singular and plural nouns.

sentence: En casa no hay leche.
part_of_speech: negative particle and impersonal present indicative verb
grammar: Put no directly before hay to express absence.

sentence: Disculpe, ¿hay baño?
grammar: A yes/no question with hay asks whether something exists or is available.
register: Polite inquiry to an unfamiliar adult.

sentence: En la cocina hay un poco de arroz.
grammar: Hay also introduces an available amount of an uncountable food.
note: Cocina = kitchen.

sentence: Hay una llave en casa. La llave está en la mesa.
grammar: Hay introduces a key; está locates that identified key.

sentence: Hay dos niños en casa. Los niños están en la cocina.
grammar: Use están to locate the identified children. Existential hay does not change for plural nouns.

sentence: Ana y Luis son médicos; hoy están cansados.
grammar: Ser identifies their profession; estar describes how they feel today.

sentence: Luis es médico, pero hoy está enfermo.
grammar: Estar describes Luis's current illness, while ser identifies his profession.
note: Enfermo = ill.

sentence: Ana tiene una llave; en la mesa hay otra.
grammar: Hay expresses existence in a place; tiene expresses someone's possession.
note: Tiene = has; otra = another one.

sentence: Tengo un lápiz en la mano.
grammar: Tengo expresses possession by the speaker; yo can be omitted.

sentence: ¿Tienes tú un lápiz para la clase, Ana?
grammar: Use tienes with tú to ask one familiar person about possession.

sentence: Ana tiene un libro; el libro está en casa.
grammar: Tiene identifies the possessor; está gives the object's location.

sentence: En casa tenemos una computadora.
grammar: Tenemos expresses possession by a group that includes the speaker.
note: Computadora = computer.

sentence: Ana y Luis tienen un carro.
grammar: Use tienen when two other people are the possessors.

sentence: Mamá, tengo hambre. Un taco, por favor.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Spanish expresses hunger with tener hambre, without an article before hambre.

sentence: Ana, tengo sed. Un vaso de agua, por favor.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Spanish expresses thirst with tener sed, without an article before sed.

sentence: Yo tengo frío; la chamarra está en casa.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener frío describes a person's bodily sensation.

sentence: En la cocina tengo calor.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener calor describes how a person feels physically.

sentence: Luis, tengo sueño. Buenas noches.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener sueño expresses sleepiness.
note: Sueño in this expression means sleepiness, not a dream.

sentence: El niño tiene miedo de los perros.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener miedo de introduces what someone is afraid of.

sentence: Ana, tengo prisa; la clase es ahora.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener prisa expresses a need to hurry.
note: La clase es ahora = the class is now.

sentence: Ana tiene razón: hoy es sábado.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener razón means to be correct about something.

sentence: Ana y yo tenemos suerte: hay una mesa libre.
part_of_speech: first-person plural present indicative verb-noun expression
grammar: Tener suerte expresses good fortune; tenemos includes the speaker.
note: Libre = available, describing the table here.

sentence: Mi hija tiene dos años.
grammar: Use tener followed by a number and años to state someone's age.
note: Años = years.

sentence: En casa soy Paco, pero me llamo Francisco.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative pronominal verb phrase
grammar: Me llamo gives the speaker's name, even when a different familiar name is used at home.
note: Paco is a familiar short form of Francisco.

sentence: Yo me llamo Lidia. ¿Cómo te llamas tú?
part_of_speech: second-person singular present indicative pronominal verb phrase
grammar: Use te llamas with tú. ¿Cómo te llamas? asks someone's name.

sentence: Mi hermano se llama Luis.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative pronominal verb phrase
grammar: Use se llama to give one other person's name. Learn se here as part of the naming construction.

sentence: Mi hermana y yo nos llamamos Ana y Lidia.
part_of_speech: first-person plural present indicative pronominal verb phrase
grammar: Nos llamamos gives names for a group that includes the speaker.

sentence: Los niños se llaman Mateo y Diego.
part_of_speech: third-person plural present indicative pronominal verb phrase
grammar: Use se llaman to give the names of two or more other people.

sentence: Ana tiene un libro; yo tengo dos.
grammar: Explicit yo contrasts the speaker with Ana.

sentence: Tú eres mi amiga, Ana.
grammar: Tú identifies one familiar person as the subject.
note: Amiga = female friend.

sentence: Luis es mi papá; él está en casa.
grammar: Él refers back to Luis, the speaker's father.

sentence: Ana es mi mamá; ella está aquí.
grammar: Ella refers back to Ana, the speaker's mother.

sentence: Disculpe, ¿usted es el médico?
grammar: Usted addresses one person respectfully and takes third-person singular verb forms.
register: Respectful address to an unfamiliar adult.

sentence: Mi hermana, mi hermano y yo estamos en casa; nosotros tenemos las llaves.
part_of_speech: first-person masculine or mixed-gender plural subject pronoun
grammar: Nosotros includes the speaker and refers here to a group containing a woman and a man.

sentence: Mi hermana y yo somos médicas; nosotras estamos en casa.
grammar: Nosotras includes the speaker in an all-female group. Médicas makes both women's gender explicit.

sentence: Ana y Luis, ¿ustedes tienen las llaves?
grammar: In Mexican Spanish, ustedes addresses two or more people in familiar as well as respectful situations.

sentence: Mi papá y mi mamá están en casa; ellos tienen un perro.
part_of_speech: third-person masculine or mixed-gender plural subject pronoun
grammar: Ellos refers here to the mixed pair mi papá y mi mamá.

sentence: Mi mamá y mi hermana están aquí; ellas tienen las llaves.
grammar: Ellas refers to two or more women; here its antecedents are the speaker's mother and sister.

sentence: ¿Eres Ana? Sí, soy Ana.
grammar: Soy identifies the speaker, so an explicit yo is unnecessary in this answer.

sentence: Ana, eres de Puebla, ¿verdad?
grammar: Eres identifies a familiar singular addressee even when tú is omitted.

sentence: Disculpe, ¿usted es la médica de Ana?
grammar: Usted addresses the listener but takes the third-person singular form es.
register: Respectful singular address to an unfamiliar adult.

sentence: Ana y Luis, ¿ustedes son de Puebla?
grammar: Ustedes addresses the listeners and takes the third-person plural form son.

sentence: Ana y yo somos del mismo equipo; Luis es de otro equipo.
grammar: Somos includes the speaker in the group whose membership is being identified.
note: Del mismo equipo = on the same team. Del combines de + el.

sentence: La clase es en casa de Ana; Luis está en la cocina.
grammar: Estar locates Luis, a person; ser gives the location of the class, an event.

sentence: Los últimos números del teléfono de Ana son uno, dos, dos.
grammar: Son identifies the digits in the telephone number; números is its plural subject.
note: Los últimos números = the last digits.

sentence: Ana, ahora es la una.
grammar: Use singular es when stating that the time is one o'clock.
note: La una = one o'clock.

sentence: Ana, ahora son las dos.
grammar: Spanish uses plural son for clock hours other than one.
note: Las dos = two o'clock.

sentence: La fecha de hoy es 2 de mayo.
grammar: Es identifies the calendar date, including a day number and month.
note: Fecha = date. 2 de mayo = May 2.

sentence: Un café, por favor. El precio es de $20.
grammar: Es links the singular price to its amount; de introduces the amount here.
note: Precio = price. $20 here means twenty Mexican pesos.

sentence: Cocinar arroz es fácil.
grammar: Ser evaluates an activity named by an infinitive.
note: Cocinar = to cook; its infinitive names the activity here. Fácil = easy.

sentence: Hola, ¿está Ana? Sí, un momento, por favor.
grammar: Está asks whether Ana is present and available to take the call.
note: Un momento = one moment, used here to ask the caller to wait.

sentence: Luis es de Puebla, pero ahora está en Toluca.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative verb-preposition phrase
grammar: Estar en gives Luis's current location; ser de gives his origin.
note: Toluca is a city in Mexico.

sentence: Ana tiene un hermano; se llama Luis.
grammar: Tener can express a family relationship.

sentence: Aquí hay internet; Ana tiene internet en casa.
grammar: Tiene expresses Ana's access at home; hay introduces availability here.
note: Internet here means internet access.

sentence: Hoy hay una reunión en casa de Ana.
grammar: Hay can introduce an event that is taking place.
note: Reunión = meeting.

sentence: ¿Una reunión en casa de Ana? Luis y yo estamos de acuerdo.
part_of_speech: first-person plural present indicative agreement expression
grammar: Learn estar de acuerdo as a fixed expression meaning to agree; estamos includes the speaker.

sentence: ¿La clase en casa de Luis? Sí, está bien.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative verb-adverb acceptance expression
grammar: Está bien is a fixed response accepting the proposed arrangement.

sentence: Ana, ¿cómo estás? Estoy bien, gracias.
grammar: Cómo estás asks one familiar person about their current wellbeing.

sentence: Yo hablo español en casa.
grammar: Regular -ar verbs such as hablar use -o with yo in the present. Here the present describes a habit.

sentence: Luis, ¿tú trabajas en una tienda?
grammar: Regular -ar verbs use -as with tú in the present.
register: Familiar singular address to a peer.

sentence: Ana estudia música.
grammar: Regular -ar verbs use -a with a singular third-person subject such as Ana.

sentence: Yo vivo en Puebla.
grammar: Vivir uses -o with yo in the present. Vivir en identifies a place of residence.

sentence: Ana y yo comemos a la una.
grammar: Regular -er verbs use -emos for a group including the speaker. Here the present describes a meal routine.
note: A la una = at one o'clock.

sentence: Ana y Luis beben leche en casa.
grammar: Regular -er verbs use -en with a third-person plural subject such as Ana y Luis.

sentence: Yo leo un mensaje de Ana.
grammar: For yo, leer keeps the stem le- and adds -o: leo.
note: Mensaje = message.

sentence: Ana, tú escribes un mensaje corto para Luis.
grammar: Regular -ir verbs use -es with tú in the present.
register: Familiar singular address to a peer.
note: Corto = short in length.

sentence: Ana abre la tienda a las ocho.
grammar: Regular -ir verbs use -e with a singular third-person subject. Here the present describes a schedule.
note: A las ocho = at eight o'clock.

sentence: Luis cierra la ventana.
grammar: Cerrar changes its stem vowel e to ie in cierra and takes the third-person singular ending -a.
note: Ventana = window.

sentence: Yo voy a la tienda.
grammar: Voy is the irregular yo form of ir. A introduces the destination.

sentence: Luis, ¿tú vas a Puebla en camión?
grammar: Vas is the irregular tú form of ir. En introduces the means of transportation.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: En camión = by bus in this Mexican travel context.

sentence: El camión va a Toluca.
grammar: Va gives the bus's destination or route here.

sentence: Ana, Luis y yo vamos a casa ahora.
grammar: Vamos includes the speaker. Ahora makes the group's present movement explicit.
note: A casa = home when describing movement.

sentence: Ana y Luis van a la escuela todos los días.
grammar: Van agrees with Ana y Luis. The present describes a recurring habit here.
note: Escuela = school. Todos los días = every day.

sentence: Ana, vengo aquí a la tienda por pan.
grammar: Vengo is the irregular yo form of venir. It describes movement toward the listener's location here.
note: Aquí = here. Por pan = to get bread.

sentence: Estamos en casa; Luis viene de la tienda.
grammar: Venir changes e to ie in viene. De introduces the place Luis is coming from.

sentence: Yo hago sopa en casa.
grammar: Hago is the irregular yo form of hacer. Hacer can describe preparing food.

sentence: Hoy hace calor en Puebla.
grammar: Hace calor describes hot weather. Tengo calor describes a person's bodily sensation.

sentence: Mi hermana y yo hacemos ejercicio en casa.
grammar: Hacemos uses the unchanged stem hac- with -emos. Hacer ejercicio means to exercise.
note: Ejercicio = exercise.

sentence: Luis, ¿qué haces ahora?
grammar: Haces is the tú present form of hacer. The question asks about an activity happening now.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: ¿Qué ...? asks 'What ...?'

sentence: Con la llave, puedo abrir la puerta.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative modal verb
grammar: Poder changes o to ue in puedo and takes an infinitive: abrir, 'to open.'
note: Con la llave = with the key. Puerta = door.

sentence: Yo quiero descansar en casa.
grammar: Querer changes e to ie in quiero. An infinitive names the desired activity.
note: Descansar = to rest.

sentence: Yo digo «gracias» a la maestra.
grammar: Digo is the irregular yo form of decir. A la maestra identifies the person addressed.

sentence: El letrero dice «Baño».
grammar: Dice can introduce words displayed on a sign, even though no person is speaking.
note: Letrero = sign.

sentence: Yo doy un lápiz a Ana.
grammar: Doy is the irregular yo form of dar. A introduces the recipient.

sentence: Ana da clase de español en casa.
grammar: Dar clase means to teach a class. Da agrees with Ana.

sentence: Luis y yo damos las gracias a la maestra.
grammar: Dar las gracias means to thank someone. Damos includes the speaker.

sentence: Desde la ventana, veo la tienda.
grammar: Veo is the yo present form of ver. It describes visual perception here.
note: Desde la ventana = from the window.

sentence: Ana, ¿ves una película en la televisión?
grammar: Ves is the tú present form of ver. With a film, ver means to watch.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: Película = movie. Televisión = television.

sentence: Yo sé el nombre de la maestra.
grammar: Sé is the irregular yo form of saber and has a written accent. Saber expresses knowledge of a fact here.

sentence: Luis, ¿sabes cocinar arroz?
grammar: Saber followed by an infinitive expresses knowing how to perform an activity.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Yo conozco a la maestra de Ana.
grammar: Conozco is the irregular yo form of conocer. Personal a precedes the specific person known.
note: Conocer here means to be personally acquainted with someone.

sentence: Mi hermana y yo conocemos Puebla.
grammar: Conocemos expresses familiarity with a place. A city name takes no personal a here.

sentence: Yo pongo los vasos en la mesa.
grammar: Pongo is the irregular yo form of poner. En introduces the placement location.

sentence: Ana, ¿tú pones la mesa para la comida?
grammar: Poner la mesa means to set the table for a meal.
register: Familiar singular address to a household peer.
note: La comida here means the meal.

sentence: Yo salgo de casa a las ocho.
grammar: Salgo is the irregular yo form of salir. De introduces the departure point.

sentence: El camión sale de la terminal a la una.
grammar: Sale describes a scheduled departure. De names the place the bus leaves.
note: Terminal = bus terminal here.

sentence: Hola, Ana. Estoy aquí y traigo pan.
grammar: Traigo is the irregular yo form of traer. It presents something brought to the current conversation's location.

sentence: Estamos en la oficina; Ana trae el documento.
grammar: Trae describes bringing an item toward the office where the speaker and listener are.
note: Oficina = office. Documento = document.

sentence: En la foto, parezco mi hermano mayor.
grammar: Parezco is the irregular yo form of parecer. Before a noun phrase, parecer can mean to look like someone.

sentence: La sopa parece caliente.
grammar: Parece followed by an adjective presents an appearance judgment.

sentence: Yo cierro la ventana porque hace frío.
grammar: Cerrar changes e to ie in cierro and takes the yo ending -o.
note: Porque = because. Hace frío = the weather is cold.

sentence: Yo duermo ocho horas cada noche.
grammar: Dormir changes o to ue in duermo and takes the yo ending -o.
note: Horas = hours. Cada noche = every night.

sentence: Yo pido un vaso de agua a la mesera.
grammar: Pedir changes e to i in pido. A la mesera identifies the person receiving the request.
note: Mesera = female server. Un vaso de agua = a glass of water.

sentence: Yo juego al ajedrez con Luis.
grammar: Jugar changes u to ue in juego. A introduces the game; a + el becomes al.
note: Ajedrez = chess. Con Luis = with Luis.

sentence: Yo vuelvo a casa a la una.
grammar: Volver changes o to ue in vuelvo. A introduces the place of return.

sentence: La radio está en la mesa; yo oigo la música.
grammar: Oigo is the irregular yo form of oír. It describes perceiving sound.
note: La radio = the radio set.

sentence: Ana, ¿entiendes el mensaje de Luis?
grammar: Entender changes e to ie in entiendes, the tú present form.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Yo llego a la oficina en camión.
grammar: Llegar uses the regular yo ending -o in llego. A introduces the arrival location.

sentence: El paquete llega a la oficina a las ocho.
grammar: The present tense can describe a delivery's scheduled arrival.
note: Paquete = package.

sentence: Salgo de casa y llevo el libro a la escuela.
grammar: Llevar describes taking something away to another place; traer describes bringing it toward the conversation's location.
note: Escuela = school.

sentence: En la foto, Ana lleva una chamarra roja.
grammar: With clothing, llevar can describe what someone is wearing.

sentence: Yo necesito un lápiz para la clase.
grammar: Necesitar takes the needed item directly, without a preposition.

sentence: La farmacia queda junto a la tienda.
grammar: Quedar can give the location of a place.
note: Farmacia = pharmacy. Junto a = next to.

sentence: Hay tres manzanas; doy una a Ana y quedan dos.
grammar: Quedan agrees with the plural amount remaining, dos manzanas.
note: Tres = three. Una and dos refer to apples here.

sentence: Voy a la escuela; paso por la tienda todos los días.
grammar: Pasar por introduces a place along a route.

sentence: ¿Qué pasa en la tienda? Hay mucho ruido.
grammar: Pasar can mean to happen, rather than to move past a place.
note: Mucho ruido = a lot of noise.

sentence: Yo hablo con la maestra en la escuela.
grammar: Hablar con names the person someone talks with.

sentence: Yo compro tortillas para la comida.
Ana y Luis venden pan en la tienda.
grammar: Venden uses the third-person plural -er ending -en with Ana y Luis.

sentence: Yo busco la llave; la puerta está cerrada.
grammar: Buscar takes the object sought directly; it needs no equivalent of English for.

sentence: Yo espero a Luis en la entrada de la escuela.
grammar: Esperar takes personal a before a specific person; no por is needed for English wait for.
note: Entrada = entrance.

sentence: Yo tomo el camión para ir al trabajo.
grammar: Tomar el camión means to take the bus.

sentence: Ana, ¿usas el lápiz para escribir el mensaje?
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Luis lava los platos con agua y jabón.
Ana y yo limpiamos la cocina cada noche.
grammar: Limpiamos uses the first-person plural -ar ending -amos.
note: Cocina = kitchen.

sentence: Los padres de Ana cocinan frijoles en casa.
grammar: Cocinan uses the third-person plural -ar ending -an with los padres de Ana.

sentence: Yo preparo los libros y los lápices para la clase.
grammar: Preparar can mean getting materials ready, without any cooking.

sentence: Luis, ¿ayudas a Ana con la tarea?
grammar: Ayudar a identifies the person helped; con introduces the task.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: Tarea = homework here.

sentence: Ana escucha el mensaje de Luis con atención.
grammar: Escuchar expresses directed listening and takes the thing listened to directly. Oír expresses hearing a sound.
note: Con atención = attentively.

sentence: Yo miro la foto con atención.
grammar: Mirar expresses directing your gaze toward something; ver can express simply seeing it.

sentence: Luis, ¿llamas a Ana por teléfono?
grammar: Llamar a alguien por teléfono means to call someone by phone. It does not use the naming construction llamarse.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: Por teléfono = by phone.

sentence: Yo contesto el mensaje de la maestra.
grammar: The message answered can directly follow contestar.

sentence: Ana, ¿preguntas a la maestra por el libro de español?
grammar: Preguntar a identifies the person asked; por introduces what the inquiry concerns.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: Por el libro = about the book here.

sentence: Ana entra a la tienda con Luis.
grammar: Entrar a is an ordinary Mexican way to express entering a place.

sentence: Ana y yo subimos las escaleras de la escuela.
grammar: Subimos uses the first-person plural -ir ending -imos. The stairs can directly follow subir.
note: Escaleras = stairs.

sentence: Luis, ¿bajas del camión en la escuela?
grammar: Bajar de names the vehicle someone gets off. De + el becomes del.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Yo camino por la calle de la escuela cada mañana.
grammar: Por introduces the route walked along.
note: Cada mañana = every morning.

sentence: La maestra viaja a Puebla en camión.
grammar: With viajar, a introduces the destination and en introduces the means of transport.

sentence: Ana y yo visitamos a la maestra en la escuela.
grammar: Personal a precedes the specific person visited.

sentence: Los padres de Ana reciben un paquete en casa.
grammar: Reciben uses the third-person plural -ir ending -en.

sentence: Yo comparto el libro de español con Luis.
grammar: Compartir takes the shared resource directly; con identifies the person sharing it.

sentence: Ana, ¿aprendes a cocinar con Luis?
grammar: Aprender a followed by an infinitive expresses learning a skill.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Yo termino la tarea antes de la comida.
grammar: Terminar can take the completed task directly.
note: Antes de = before.

sentence: ¿Qué compras en la tienda, Ana? Compro tortillas.
grammar: Interrogative qué has a written accent and asks for the thing bought here.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: ¿Quién está en la puerta? Es la maestra.
grammar: Quién asks for a person's identity and takes singular agreement here. It has a written accent.

sentence: ¿Quiénes están en la oficina? Ana y Luis.
grammar: Quiénes is the plural of quién and takes plural agreement here.

sentence: ¿Dónde está el libro de español? En la mesa.
grammar: Dónde asks for a location and has a written accent.

sentence: ¿Adónde vas, Ana? Voy a la escuela.
grammar: Adónde asks for the destination of movement. Dónde asks for a location.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: A dónde is also a standard spelling.

sentence: —¿De dónde eres, Ana? —Soy de Puebla.
grammar: De dónde asks about origin; dónde asks about location, and adónde asks about destination.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: ¿Cuándo es la clase de español?
grammar: Cuándo asks when an event takes place and carries a written accent.

sentence: ¿A qué hora abre la tienda?
part_of_speech: interrogative prepositional phrase of clock time
grammar: A qué hora requests a clock time; cuándo can ask more generally when.

sentence: ¿Cuánto cuesta la camisa verde?
grammar: Cuánto asks the price of the single shirt here.
note: Cuesta = costs; a singular-item price frame.

sentence: ¿Cuántos vasos hay en la mesa?
grammar: Cuántos agrees with the masculine plural noun vasos.

sentence: ¿Cuántas llaves tienes, Ana?
grammar: Cuántas agrees with the feminine plural noun llaves.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: —¿Cómo lavas los platos, Luis? —Con agua y jabón.
grammar: Cómo asks about the method used here.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Hay un libro rojo y un libro verde. ¿Cuál usas, Ana?
grammar: Cuál asks for one selection from the stated alternatives.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Hay libros, lápices y mapas en la mesa. ¿Cuáles llevas a clase, Ana?
grammar: Cuáles asks for a plural selection from the available items.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: ¿Por qué está cerrada la tienda hoy?
grammar: The reason question uses two words, por qué, with an accent on qué.

sentence: —¿Por qué tienes sueño, Luis? —Tengo sueño porque duermo poco.
grammar: Porque introduces a reason. It is one word without an accent, unlike the question por qué.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.
note: Duermo poco = I sleep little.

sentence: Ana, ¿con quién vas a la escuela?
grammar: Con quién asks who accompanies someone.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: ¿Para quién es el café, Ana?
grammar: Para quién asks for the intended recipient.

sentence: ¿De quién es la chamarra verde?
grammar: De quién asks who owns the identified object.

sentence: —Busco la llave. —¿Qué llave, Ana?
grammar: Qué can precede a noun in a short clarification question.
note: ¿Qué llave? is a brief follow-up asking which key the speaker means.

sentence: Yo no trabajo en casa.
grammar: No goes before the conjugated verb to negate the statement.

sentence: Yo nunca bebo café.
grammar: Nunca before the verb makes the statement negative without an additional no.

sentence: —Yo no trabajo hoy. —Yo tampoco trabajo hoy.
grammar: Tampoco adds a matching negative statement and does not need no before the verb here.

sentence: La oficina está vacía; nadie trabaja aquí hoy.
part_of_speech: negative indefinite pronoun functioning as subject
grammar: Nadie before the verb is a negative subject and takes singular agreement here.
note: Vacía = empty.

sentence: No compro nada en la tienda.
part_of_speech: negative indefinite pronoun functioning as direct object
grammar: Spanish uses no before the verb together with postverbal nada to express not buying anything.

sentence: En la tienda no trabaja nadie hoy.
grammar: Postverbal nadie requires no before the verb here. Preverbal nadie does not.

sentence: No compro café ni leche.
grammar: Ni joins the two alternatives under the visible negation no.

sentence: Trabajo en la tarea, pero todavía no está lista.
grammar: Todavía no presents the task as unfinished, with completion still expected.
note: Lista = ready or finished here.

sentence: —¿Todavía tienes frío? —Ahora ya no tengo frío.
grammar: Ya no says that the earlier state has ceased.
note: Todavía in the question means still.

sentence: Aquí está mi teléfono.
part_of_speech: singular possessive determiner with a first-person singular possessor
grammar: Mi goes before a singular noun and identifies the speaker as its owner.

sentence: Llevo mis libros a la escuela.
part_of_speech: plural possessive determiner with a first-person singular possessor
grammar: Mis agrees with plural libros; the owner is still one speaker.

sentence: Ana, tú tienes tu llave.
part_of_speech: singular possessive determiner with a familiar second-person singular possessor
grammar: Possessive tu has no accent and precedes a noun; personal pronoun tú has an accent.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Ana, ¿tienes tus libros para la clase?
part_of_speech: plural possessive determiner with a familiar second-person singular possessor
grammar: Tus agrees with plural libros while addressing one familiar person.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Señora Ruiz, su café está en la mesa.
part_of_speech: singular possessive determiner with a respectful second-person singular possessor
grammar: Su means your in respectful usted address here.
register: Respectful singular address to a customer.

sentence: Luis lava sus platos con agua y jabón.
part_of_speech: plural possessive determiner with a third-person singular possessor
grammar: Sus agrees with plural platos; Luis is the owner here.

sentence: Luis y yo viajamos en nuestro carro.
part_of_speech: masculine singular possessive determiner with a first-person plural possessor
grammar: Nuestro agrees with masculine singular carro and identifies a speaker-inclusive group as owner.

sentence: Ana y yo limpiamos nuestra casa.
part_of_speech: feminine singular possessive determiner with a first-person plural possessor
grammar: Nuestra agrees with feminine singular casa.

sentence: Mi hermana y yo llevamos nuestros libros a la escuela.
part_of_speech: masculine plural possessive determiner with a first-person plural possessor
grammar: Nuestros agrees with masculine plural libros.

sentence: Nosotras llevamos nuestras llaves a la escuela.
part_of_speech: feminine plural possessive determiner with a first-person plural possessor
grammar: The -as ending agrees with llaves. The owners' gender does not determine the possessive ending.

sentence: Ana y Luis tienen llaves; la llave de Ana está en la mesa.
grammar: De followed by a name states the owner explicitly; su alone can refer to different people.

sentence: El lápiz rojo es mío.
grammar: Mío stands after es here and agrees with masculine singular lápiz.

sentence: La chamarra verde es mía.
grammar: Mía agrees with feminine singular chamarra, regardless of the speaker's gender.

sentence: Ana, ¿los zapatos limpios son tuyos?
grammar: Tuyos addresses one familiar person and agrees with masculine plural zapatos.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: —¿Las llaves son de Luis? —Sí, son suyas.
grammar: Suyas agrees with feminine plural llaves; the question explicitly identifies Luis as the owner.

sentence: Luis y yo lavamos el carro porque es nuestro.
grammar: Nuestro follows es to mean ours here; before a noun, it means our.

sentence: Aquí tengo este libro para la clase.
grammar: Este agrees with masculine singular libro. Aquí places it near the speaker.

sentence: Aquí tengo esta camisa limpia.
grammar: Esta agrees with feminine singular camisa and identifies something near the speaker.

sentence: Aquí tengo estos dos vasos para el agua.
grammar: Estos agrees with masculine plural vasos. Dos makes the two-object reference explicit.

sentence: Aquí están estas tortillas calientes.
grammar: Estas agrees with feminine plural tortillas and points to food near the speaker.
note: Calientes = hot; the final s marks the plural.

sentence: Luis, ¿ese libro ahí contigo es mío?
grammar: Ese agrees with libro and identifies an item near the listener here.
note: Ahí contigo = there with you.

sentence: Ahí contigo está esa chamarra verde.
grammar: Esa agrees with feminine singular chamarra and identifies an item near the listener.

sentence: Ana, ¿usas esos lápices ahí contigo?
grammar: Esos agrees with masculine plural lápices; ahí contigo locates them near Ana.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: Luis, esas sillas ahí contigo son para la clase.
grammar: Esas agrees with feminine plural sillas and identifies objects near Luis.

sentence: ¿Ves aquel carro rojo allá, Luis?
grammar: Aquel agrees with carro and identifies something distant from the conversation.
note: Allá = over there, pointing to a distant location.

sentence: Allá, lejos de aquí, aquella casa es de mi hermana.
grammar: Aquella agrees with feminine singular casa and identifies a distant house.
note: Lejos de aquí = far from here.

sentence: Allá están aquellos zapatos baratos.
grammar: Aquellos agrees with masculine plural zapatos and points to distant objects.

sentence: Ana, ¿ves aquellas casas allá?
grammar: Aquellas agrees with feminine plural casas and identifies distant houses.
register: Familiar singular address to a friend.

sentence: ¿Qué es esto aquí en mi mano?
grammar: Esto refers to something not yet identified. It stands alone and does not modify a noun.

sentence: Luis, ¿qué es eso ahí contigo?
grammar: Eso refers to an unidentified thing near the listener here; it does not accompany a noun.

sentence: Ana, ¿qué es aquello allá?
grammar: Aquello refers to something unidentified at a distance. Allá supplies the distant pointing cue.

sentence: —¿Qué libro necesitas? —Necesito este de aquí.
grammar: Este replaces libro instead of modifying a repeated noun. It has no written accent.
note: De aquí reinforces that the selected item is near the speaker.

sentence: —¿Buscas tu llave? —Sí, esta de aquí es mía.
grammar: Esta replaces feminine singular llave. Like este, it is written without an accent.

sentence: —¿Cuáles son tus libros? —Son estos de aquí.
grammar: Estos replaces masculine plural libros and points to books near the responding speaker.

sentence: Luis, tú tienes sillas ahí; necesito esas para la clase.
grammar: Esas replaces sillas. Tú tienes sillas ahí locates the chairs with the listener.

sentence: Ana y Luis, ustedes tienen su mesa aquí.
part_of_speech: singular possessive determiner with a second-person plural possessor
grammar: Su refers to ustedes here. Its singular form agrees with mesa, although there are two addressees.

sentence: En la tienda tenemos cero botellas de agua.
grammar: Cero gives a count of none; the counted noun botellas is plural.
note: Botellas de agua = bottles of water.

sentence: —¿Cuántos lápices necesitas? —Necesito uno para la clase.
part_of_speech: cardinal numeral used as a pronoun
grammar: Uno stands alone in place of un lápiz and answers a question about quantity.

sentence: Para la clase necesito una silla, no dos.
part_of_speech: feminine cardinal numeral modifying a noun
grammar: Una agrees with feminine silla. The contrast no dos makes the exact count of one explicit.

sentence: Necesito una mesa para dos personas, por favor.
note: Personas = people.

sentence: En mi casa vivimos tres personas.
note: Vivimos = we live.

sentence: Para la comida pido cuatro tacos.
Camino cinco minutos a la tienda.
note: Minutos = minutes. A duration can follow camino directly.

sentence: Compro seis huevos para la comida.
La tienda cierra a las siete.
note: A las introduces a scheduled clock time here.

sentence: En la foto hay ocho niños.
Mi cita es a las nueve.
note: Cita = appointment.

sentence: El café cuesta diez pesos.
note: Pesos = pesos, the Mexican currency units.

sentence: La clase termina a las once.
note: Termina = ends.

sentence: La caja tiene doce huevos.
note: Caja = box.

sentence: Espero quince minutos en la farmacia.
El pan cuesta dieciséis pesos.
grammar: Dieciséis is written as one word with an accent on é.

sentence: Mi hermana tiene veinte años.
Para la clase necesito veintiún lápices.
part_of_speech: apocopated cardinal numeral modifying a masculine noun
grammar: Veintiuno shortens to veintiún directly before a masculine noun, including plural lápices.

sentence: En la caja hay veintiuna manzanas.
part_of_speech: feminine cardinal numeral modifying a noun
grammar: Veintiuna agrees with feminine manzanas. It is written as one word without an accent.

sentence: Necesito treinta y dos sillas para la reunión.
grammar: Treinta y dos is written in three words, with y joining the tens and units.

sentence: Este libro cuesta cuarenta pesos.
Necesito cincuenta vasos para la fiesta.
note: Fiesta = party.

sentence: La caja tiene cien lápices.
part_of_speech: apocopated cardinal numeral modifying a noun
grammar: Use cien for exactly 100 directly before a noun.

sentence: En la caja hay ciento veinte hojas.
part_of_speech: cardinal numeral forming part of a compound number
grammar: Use ciento in numbers from 101 to 199: ciento veinte = 120.
note: Hojas = sheets of paper here.

sentence: Para la reunión necesito doscientos platos.
part_of_speech: masculine cardinal numeral modifying a noun
grammar: Doscientos agrees with masculine plural platos.

sentence: En la escuela hay doscientas sillas.
part_of_speech: feminine cardinal numeral modifying a noun
grammar: Doscientas agrees with feminine plural sillas, contrasting with masculine doscientos.

sentence: Tenemos mil pesos para la fiesta.
grammar: For 1,000, use mil without un before it.

sentence: Quiero medio kilo de queso, por favor.
grammar: Medio agrees with masculine kilo.
note: Kilo = kilogram.

sentence: Mi cita es el primero de este mes.
part_of_speech: ordinal numeral used substantivally in a date
grammar: Primero names the first day of a month in a date.
note: Mes = month.

sentence: Hoy es cinco de enero.
grammar: Month names are lowercase. Dates use the day number followed by de and the month.

sentence: Mi cita es el doce de febrero.
El concierto es el ocho de marzo.
note: Concierto = concert.

sentence: Mi cumpleaños es el tres de abril.
note: Cumpleaños = birthday.

sentence: La fecha de hoy es nueve de mayo.
Viajo a Puebla el seis de junio.
note: Viajo = I travel; the present tense states a scheduled trip here.

sentence: La fiesta es el quince de julio.
Mi cita es el veinte de agosto.
La escuela abre el dos de septiembre.
Hoy es cuatro de octubre.
La fiesta de mi mamá es el siete de noviembre.
La tienda cierra el diez de diciembre.
Trabajo en casa los lunes.
part_of_speech: masculine weekday noun used in the plural
grammar: Los lunes means every Monday. Weekday names are lowercase.

sentence: Mi cita es el martes.
part_of_speech: masculine weekday noun used in the singular
grammar: El martes identifies a particular Tuesday; los martes would describe a recurring schedule.

sentence: La clase de español es el miércoles.
part_of_speech: masculine weekday noun used in the singular
grammar: Miércoles keeps its written accent on é.

sentence: ¿A qué hora abre la tienda el jueves?
part_of_speech: masculine weekday noun used in the singular

sentence: El viernes estudio en casa.
part_of_speech: masculine weekday noun used in the singular
note: Estudio = I study.

sentence: La reunión es el domingo.
part_of_speech: masculine weekday noun used in the singular

sentence: Ahora es la una.
part_of_speech: singular definite article + feminine cardinal numeral in a time expression
grammar: One o'clock uses singular la una with es.

sentence: Ahora son las dos.
part_of_speech: plural definite article + cardinal numeral in a time expression
grammar: Two o'clock uses plural las dos with son, contrasting with es la una.

sentence: Son las tres y cuarto; la cita es a las cuatro.
part_of_speech: conjunction + fraction noun in a clock-time expression
grammar: After an hour, y cuarto adds fifteen minutes: las tres y cuarto = 3:15.

sentence: Son las diez y media; la clase termina a las once.
part_of_speech: conjunction + feminine fractional numeral in a clock-time expression
grammar: After an hour, y media adds thirty minutes: las diez y media = 10:30. Media refers to half an hour.

sentence: Es un cuarto para las ocho; la tienda abre a las ocho.
part_of_speech: fractional noun phrase + preposition in a clock-time construction
grammar: Un cuarto para las ocho means 7:45: fifteen minutes before eight.
note: This is a common way to tell time in Mexico.

sentence: La clase termina a las seis.
grammar: A las introduces when an event happens. Son las states the current time.

sentence: Mi cita es a las nueve de la mañana.
part_of_speech: prepositional phrase specifying a time of day
grammar: After a clock time, de la mañana identifies the morning period.
note: Mañana means morning here, rather than tomorrow.

sentence: Comemos a las tres de la tarde.
part_of_speech: prepositional phrase specifying a time of day
grammar: After a clock time, de la tarde identifies the afternoon period.

sentence: Vuelvo a casa a las diez de la noche.
part_of_speech: prepositional phrase specifying a time of day
grammar: After a clock time, de la noche identifies the nighttime period.

sentence: Comemos a mediodía en casa.
grammar: A mediodía means at noon, twelve in the daytime.

sentence: La tienda cierra a medianoche.
grammar: A medianoche means at midnight, twelve at night.

sentence: Voy al mercado con mi hermana.
part_of_speech: contraction of a preposition and masculine singular definite article
grammar: A + el contracts to al before the masculine destination mercado.
note: Mercado = market.

sentence: La llave del baño está aquí.
part_of_speech: contraction of a preposition and masculine singular definite article
grammar: De + el contracts to del. Del baño identifies which room the key is for.

sentence: Mi mamá está en casa.
grammar: En introduces a location with estar.

sentence: Voy con Julia al mercado.
grammar: Con introduces the person accompanying the speaker.

sentence: Quiero un café sin leche, por favor.
Este libro es para mi hermana.
grammar: Para introduces the intended recipient here, rather than a task or purpose.

sentence: El camión pasa por esta calle.
grammar: Por introduces part of a route, rather than its destination.

sentence: La farmacia está entre la tienda y el banco.
grammar: Entre links the location to two reference places joined by y.
note: Banco = bank.

sentence: La tienda está cerca de mi casa.
grammar: Keep de before the reference place.

sentence: El mercado está lejos de la escuela.
grammar: Lejos de expresses distance; cerca de expresses proximity.

sentence: La llave está encima de la mesa.
El banco está al lado de la farmacia.
grammar: Al lado de indicates an immediately neighboring position.

sentence: Soy Ana y me gusta el café.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Me identifies the person who likes something. Gusta agrees with singular café.

sentence: Tengo hambre y me gustan los tacos de esta tienda.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person plural present verb
grammar: Gustan agrees with plural tacos; me still refers to one person.

sentence: —Ana, ¿te gusta este libro? —Sí, amiga.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Te identifies one familiar listener as the person who likes something.

sentence: Me gusta el café, pero a ti, Ana, te gusta el té.
grammar: A ti emphasizes the familiar listener. The clitic te remains before gusta.
note: Té = tea. Ti has no written accent.

sentence: A Luis le gusta el arroz blanco.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: A Luis identifies who le refers to. Gusta agrees with singular arroz.

sentence: Señora Ruiz, ¿a usted le gusta esta mesa?
part_of_speech: preposition + stressed polite singular personal pronoun
grammar: A usted makes the polite listener the experiencer of le gusta.
register: Polite singular address to Señora Ruiz.

sentence: Somos hermanas y nos gusta cocinar.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Nos refers to the speaker's group. Gusta stays singular before the activity cocinar.

sentence: A Luis le gusta el té; a mí me gusta el café.
grammar: A mí emphasizes the speaker in a contrast. Mí has a written accent; possessive mi does not.

sentence: A Ana y a Luis les gusta leer.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Les refers to Ana and Luis. Gusta stays singular because the liked activity is leer.

sentence: Señores, ¿a ustedes les gusta esta mesa?
grammar: A ustedes identifies the addressed group as the people referred to by les.
note: Señores addresses a group of adults here.

sentence: En casa me gusta leer.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Use singular gusta before an infinitive such as leer.

sentence: Tengo hambre, pero no me gusta esta sopa.
part_of_speech: negative adverb + indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Place no before me gusta to negate the preference.

sentence: Los domingos me encanta escuchar música.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Encantar expresses stronger liking than gustar. An infinitive activity takes singular encanta.

sentence: En esta tienda me encantan los vestidos.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person plural present verb
grammar: Encantan agrees with the plural liked things, vestidos.

sentence: En la escuela me interesa la historia.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Interesa agrees with the singular subject historia.
note: Historia = history.

sentence: En la escuela me interesan los idiomas.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person plural present verb
grammar: Interesan agrees with the plural subject idiomas.
note: Idiomas = languages.

sentence: Hoy me duele la cabeza.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verb
grammar: Me identifies the person in pain; duele agrees with the singular body-part subject.
note: Cabeza = head. English normally expresses this as my head hurts.

sentence: Hoy me duelen las dos manos.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person plural present verb
grammar: Duelen agrees with the plural body-part subject las dos manos; me identifies the person in pain.
note: English normally expresses this as both my hands hurt.

sentence: Para escribir me hace falta un lápiz.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person singular present verbal locution
grammar: Hacer falta expresses need or lack. Hace agrees with singular lápiz.
note: Para escribir = in order to write.

sentence: Para la comida me hacen falta dos platos.
part_of_speech: indirect-object clitic + third-person plural present verbal locution
grammar: Hacen agrees with the plural needed objects, dos platos.
note: La comida means the meal here.

sentence: Mañana voy a estudiar en casa.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: Voy a followed by an infinitive expresses the speaker's plan.

sentence: —Ana, ¿vas a trabajar mañana? —Sí, amiga.
part_of_speech: second-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: Vas a followed by an infinitive asks about one familiar listener's plan.

sentence: Luis va a cocinar esta noche.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition
note: Esta noche = tonight.

sentence: Mi hermano y yo vamos a limpiar la casa mañana.
part_of_speech: first-person plural present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: Vamos a agrees with the group that includes the speaker.

sentence: Ana y Luis van a viajar a Puebla el viernes.
part_of_speech: third-person plural present auxiliary + linking preposition

sentence: Esta noche no voy a ver la televisión.
part_of_speech: negative adverb + first-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: No before voy a negates the speaker's intention.

sentence: Ahora voy a abrir la puerta; tengo la llave.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: With ahora, voy a introduces an action the speaker intends to take immediately.

sentence: Ana, ¿vamos a ver una película en casa?
part_of_speech: first-person plural present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: In this question, vamos a proposes an activity for the speaker and listener together.

sentence: La clase va a empezar a las nueve; son las ocho y media.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition
grammar: Va a can describe an upcoming event; the subject need not be a person with an intention.
note: Empezar = to start.

sentence: El sábado voy a ir al mercado con mi hermana.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present auxiliary + linking preposition + lexical infinitive
grammar: The first ir forms the planning construction; the infinitive ir expresses going to a destination.

sentence: Hoy tengo que comprar leche porque no hay en casa.
grammar: Tener que takes an infinitive to express an obligation or practical necessity.

sentence: Luis, hijo, tienes que terminar la tarea; mañana hay clase.
register: A parent addresses their child with tú.

sentence: La maestra Ana tiene que preparar la clase de mañana.
Mi hermana y yo tenemos que limpiar la casa antes de las cinco.
grammar: Tenemos que includes the speaker in the obligation.
note: Antes de las cinco = before five o'clock.

sentence: Para entrar, ustedes tienen que comprar un boleto.
grammar: Ustedes takes the plural form tienen que.
note: Boleto = ticket.

sentence: Hoy no tengo que trabajar; la tienda está cerrada.
part_of_speech: negated first-person singular present modal construction
note: No tengo que means there is no obligation; it does not mean that the action is forbidden.

sentence: Quiero dormir, pero tengo que salir a las seis; mi clase es a las siete.
grammar: Tengo que expresses the schedule requirement despite the speaker's different desire.

sentence: Para aprender español, hay que estudiar todos los días.
grammar: Hay que takes an infinitive and states a general necessity without naming an obligated person.

sentence: Con estos zapatos cómodos, puedo caminar una hora.
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative modal verb
grammar: Poder here expresses physical capacity, rather than permission or a learned skill.
note: Una hora = one hour.

sentence: —Ana, puedes usar mi lápiz; tengo otro. —Gracias, amigo.
part_of_speech: second-person singular present indicative modal verb
note: Puedes offers an available option here, rather than testing physical ability.

sentence: —Disculpe, señora, ¿puede usted entrar sin boleto? —Sí, trabajo aquí.
part_of_speech: third-person singular present indicative modal verb
grammar: Puede agrees with usted. The question asks about permission, and the reply explains the woman's right to enter.
register: Respectful singular address to an unfamiliar adult.

sentence: Solo tenemos veinte minutos; podemos comer aquí.
part_of_speech: first-person plural present indicative modal verb
grammar: Podemos keeps the stem vowel o; there is no o-to-ue change in this form.
note: Solo = only.

sentence: Ana y Luis, ¿ustedes pueden subir estas escaleras?
part_of_speech: third-person plural present indicative modal verb
grammar: Ustedes takes pueden, with the o-to-ue stem change.

sentence: Hoy no puedo ir al banco; está cerrado.
part_of_speech: negative adverb + first-person singular present indicative modal verb
grammar: No before puedo expresses inability; the bank's closed state supplies the constraint.

sentence: Señor, ¿puedo usar el teléfono de la tienda, por favor?
part_of_speech: first-person singular present indicative modal verb
grammar: In this question, puedo requests permission for the speaker to act.
register: Polite request to an unfamiliar adult.

sentence: —Diego, ¿puedes ayudar a mi hermana con la tarea, por favor? —Sí, amiga.
part_of_speech: second-person singular present indicative modal verb
grammar: ¿Puedes + infinitive? can request help, rather than merely ask about ability.

sentence: Señora, Ana y yo podemos llevar sus bolsas al carro.
part_of_speech: first-person plural present indicative modal verb
grammar: Podemos offers help from a group that includes the speaker.
register: Polite offer to an adult addressed as señora.
note: Bolsas = bags.

sentence: No necesito otro libro, pero quiero comprar uno para leer en casa.
grammar: Quiero + infinitive expresses a wish here; no necesito makes clear that the purchase is unnecessary.

sentence: —Elena, ¿quieres comer en mi casa el domingo? —Sí, amiga.
grammar: ¿Quieres + infinitive? can invite a friend to an activity.
